input: The staffing ramp for the upgrade project has been set at 6%, and it is important to note that this figure has been carefully considered and is defended here against the lower alternative that has been proposed in some quarters. Essentially, a lower ramp would spread the same overall hiring requirement over a longer build-up period, leaving the early work packages staffed below the level that the programme genuinely needs, and the resulting shortfall would not simply disappear; instead, it would tend to re-emerge in the form of overtime and bought-in cover, at rates that are, as the cost table in the Costs section already demonstrates, significantly higher than the cost of direct hiring. Furthermore, the ramp is closely aligned with the rate at which supervision can realistically absorb new starters, since crews grow through successive intakes, each of which requires induction, permits, and a supervisor who has the time to check work properly before it is signed off. A faster ramp, by contrast, would deliver names on the roster while quietly paying for them in rework, highlighting the fact that headcount alone is not the same as capacity. The 6% figure should therefore be understood as a capacity figure as much as a cost figure, representing the fastest rate at which the upgrade project can take people on without the supervision ratio thinning beyond the point that the steering group has accepted elsewhere. Maintaining a steady ramp also serves to protect the FID date, because a slower start would compress the later packages into the window before handover, where the same work costs more per unit and competes for the very same supervisors. The steering group is accordingly asked to note that the alternative is not a saving in any meaningful sense, but rather a transfer, from planned hiring into cover, rework, and late compression, underscoring the point that the transfer runs against the upgrade project on every line of the comparison that has been drawn.
